title: egress-failover-and-nat-swap-playbook-for-gpu-tenant-pools
author: Priya Nair
content:
Summary:

This playbook captures the operational pattern, Terraform/IaC module design, CI/CD canary sequence, and on-call runbook for automated egress-path failover and NAT gateway swap for GPU tenant pools. It is intended for platform engineers who operate multi-tenant GPU clusters and need fast, reliable egress failover while preserving cost controls and networking isolation.

Goal and constraints:

- Goal: provide sub-60s failover of tenant egress traffic during NAT/GW or peering failures while keeping per-tenant billing attribution intact and avoiding broad route flaps.
- Constraints: must work across AWS and GCP account topologies we operate; must tolerate preemptible/spot host churn; minimum required changes to tenant VPC routing tables; Terraform-driven to allow safe rollout and rollback.

Scope and audience:

- Scope: GPU tenant egress for inference/eval workloads and build/test sandboxes. Does NOT cover private customer VPNs or inter-region data replication paths.
- Audience: infra, SRE, platform, private-deployments engineers.

High-level design overview:

1) Dual-path egress model
- Primary egress: per-tenant NAT gateway (or cloud NAT) in the tenant account/namespace, used for regular production traffic.
- Secondary egress: central shared egress fabric (account-owned egress fleet) with per-tenant SNAT pools and strict RBAC to ensure isolation.
- Failover trigger: health checks (BGP adj, NAT metrics, dataplane probes) or scheduled maintenance that flips a tenancy-specific route or BGP prepend.

2) Failure domains and isolation
- Per-tenant route objects or prefix-lists are modified rather than touching global route tables.
- Use of stateful firewall rules + subnet-level egress ACLs to ensure traffic cannot escape during partial failover.

3) Observability and SLOs
- SLO: 99.9% of egress connectivity events recover within 60 seconds for requests that cross the egress fabric.
- Metrics to emit: nat-healthy (bool), snat-utilization (p50/p90), egress-latency-ms (p50/p95), pkt-loss-percent, bgp-adj-state.
- Alerts: nat-down (5m), bgp-flap (3 occurrences in 1m), sudden-snat-utilization-spike (>80% sustained 2m).

Terraform / IaC module pattern:

We provide two modules to keep responsibilities clear:

- module: tenant-egress-nat (tenant-owned)
  - Responsibilities: provision NAT gateway / Cloud NAT in tenant account, allocate elastic IP(s) (AWS) or static external IPs (GCP), attach health-check target group and dataplane probe configuration.
  - Inputs: tenant_id, subnet_ids (list), preferred_eips (list, optional), failover_priority (int).
  - Outputs: nat_ips (list), nat_id (string), nat_health_check_endpoint (string).

- module: central-egress-fabric
  - Responsibilities: provision central NAT fleet (autoscaling pool), SNAT pool allocation mechanism, per-tenant SNAT mapping table, BGP session templates for peering fabric, and IAM roles that allow tenant accounts to register failover routes.
  - Inputs: fabric_region, snat_pool_size, bgp_asn, tenant_registration_role_arn.
  - Outputs: fabric_vpn, bgp_peer_status_endpoint, snat_allocations (map).

Example Terraform usage snippet (simplified):

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.4"
}
module "tenant_abc_nat" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.redwood.internal/infra/terraform-modules.git//tenant-egress-nat?ref=v1.2.0"
  tenant_id = "tenant-abc"
  subnet_ids = ["subnet-0ab12c3d", "subnet-0cd34ef5"]
  preferred_eips = []
}

module "central_egress" {
  source = "git::ssh://git.redwood.internal/infra/terraform-modules.git//central-egress-fabric?ref=v1.0.1"
  fabric_region = "us-west-2"
  snat_pool_size = 256
  bgp_asn = 64512
  tenant_registration_role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::111222333444:role/egress-registration"
}

Automated failover choreography (CI/CD + control plane):

Overview: a small control-plane service (egress-orchestrator) performs the failover sequence when a health signal is received. All changes must be approved by the canary pipeline before being applied at scale.

Failover sequence (tenant-scoped):
1) Detect: health probe for tenant NAT fails (3 consecutive probes, 10s interval) OR BGP session goes down.
2) Validate: egress-orchestrator fetches last-known NAT metrics and verifies not a transient spike.
3) Lock: create a terraform state lock and write a tenant failover marker in central key-value store (etcd/consul).
4) Canary execution: apply Terraform to attach tenant route to central-egress SNAT pool for a single subnet (canary-subnet).
5) Smoke tests: run short HTTP/S/ICMP probes from the canary-subnet to 3rd-party endpoints and internal egress test endpoints.
6) Promote: if canary succeeded, apply Terraform changes across remaining subnets for the tenant.
7) Audit and metrics: emit event to audit log, increment egress-failover-counter, write rollback snapshot.
8) Cleanup: release any temporary EIPs and remove the tenant failover marker.

Canary gating policy:
- Maximum rate: 1 tenant canary per region concurrently.
- Success criteria: 3/3 probe endpoints successful for 30s and no packet loss >0.5%.
- Automatic rollback window: 5 minutes after canary promotion if any critical error.

CI/CD pipeline hooks and safety nets:

- Pipeline stages: plan -> canary-apply -> probe -> promote-apply -> post-checks -> notify.
- Approvals: service account runs plan/canary-apply; promote-apply requires oncall or platform lead approval for cross-account changes unless a TTL-free failover marker exists.
- Abort conditions: terraform-plan shows >1 production route object change outside tenant scope; SNAT pool would exceed allocation limit; plan includes global route table modifications.

Runbook: Oncall steps for a NAT outage affecting GPU inference tenants

1) Triage
- Check alerts in PagerDuty and corresponding Grafana dashboards.
- Confirm nat-healthy=false for tenant id(s) in the last 5m.
- Check BGP peer status page: bgp-adj-state for fabric.

2) Immediate mitigation (if automated failover hasn't triggered)
- From control-plane (ssh to egress-orchestrator pod): curl -X POST /v1/failover/tenant/tenant-abc
- This will create a terraform plan in a build artifact and perform a canary-apply against the canary subnet.

3) If canary fails
- Re-run smoke probes with tcpdump on the canary-subnet host to examine SNAT translation and TCP resets.
- Check SNAT allocation saturation: query central_egress_admin CLI: redwood-egress-admin snat-utilization --tenant tenant-abc
- If saturation > 85% and failure persists, increase snat_pool_size for tenant by creating a quickpatch terraform change (fast path: add one /27 worth of SNATs) and run promote-apply.

4) Full rollback
- If promote-apply introduced regressions and cannot be fixed within 10m, revert via terraform state snapshot saved in S3. Command:

aws s3 cp s3://terraform-state-backups/egress/tenant-tenant-abc/latest-snapshot.tfstate ./rollback.tfstate
terraform init
terraform state replace-provider --state=./rollback.tfstate old-provider new-provider
terraform apply -state=./rollback.tfstate -auto-approve

5) Post-incident actions
- Create an incident in the incident tracker with summary, timeline, impact list (tenants affected), root cause hypothesis.
- Assign RCA owner and schedule deep-dive within 72 hours.
- Add regression test to nightly egress-e2e pipeline if issue was undetected by probes.

Troubleshooting matrix (quick reference):

- Symptom: NAT metrics show healthy=true but tenants report 502s
  - Check: application-level connection limits on NAT instances (conntrack).
  - Fix: rotate nat host or increase conntrack_max via SSM/GCP equivalent; consider adding more NAT hosts to autoscaling group.

- Symptom: High SNAT reuse (many different tenant flows sharing one IP)
  - Check: SNAT pool allocation map for tenant; verify port exhaustion on EIPs.
  - Fix: allocate additional SNAT IPs or reduce ephemeral port consumption in client configs.

- Symptom: BGP flaps when promoting tenant route
  - Check: AS path length and prepend operations; verify dampening settings on peer.
  - Fix: throttle prefix changes, increase hold-time, and retry promotion with smaller batch sizes.

Operational run frequency and tests:

- Daily: egress health probes and SNAT utilization snapshot stored in time-series for 30 days.
- Weekly: restore-from-backup drill for one tenant state (exercise terraform state restore).
- Monthly: canary-failover simulation (dry run) for 5% of tenants using synthetic traffic.
- Quarterly: cross-account peering failover DR test with SRE and networking on-call present.

Security and compliance considerations:

- All cross-account role assumptions use short-lived credentials (STS) and are audited.
- Key rotation: EIP association events and SNAT mapping changes must be logged to audit S3 with encryption (KMS key: arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:111222333444:key/egress-audit).
- Customers with data residency restrictions: restricted tenants must use tenant-owned NAT only; central failover can be disabled per-tenant with tenant flag in registration table.

Appendix: example smoke test script (bash)

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
TENANT=${1:-tenant-abc}
CANARY_HOST=10.0.11.5 # internal canary-subnet host
ENDPOINTS=(https://example.com https://httpbin.org/ip https://internal-egress-test.redwood.internal/echo)
for url in "${ENDPOINTS[@]}"; do
  echo "Probing ${url} from ${CANARY_HOST}"
  kubectl exec -n infra-tests canary-pod -- curl -sS -m 10 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' "$url" || { echo "probe failed to $url"; exit 2; }
done

echo "all probes passed"
